opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because PINNs got a lot of excitement early on, and I think it's important to be clear about where they struggle.

The core idea of a physics-informed neural network is that you take a neural network, treat it as the solution function itself, and add the PDE residual into the loss. So you're essentially solving one instance of the problem by optimization. That's elegant, but it brings a few fundamental limitations, and they get much worse for time-dependent problems.

The first is the optimization landscape. When you put the PDE residual into the loss, you get a very ill-conditioned problem. The different terms (the boundary conditions, the initial conditions, the residual in the interior) compete with each other, and the gradients can be badly imbalanced. For time-evolving systems, especially chaotic or multiscale ones like turbulent fluid flow, errors in the early part of the trajectory propagate, and the network often converges to a trivial or wrong solution that still has a deceptively small residual. People have tried curriculum training, causal weighting in time, and adaptive loss balancing, and those help, but they're patches on a hard optimization problem.

The second is spectral bias. Standard neural networks tend to learn smooth, low-frequency functions first. Many physical phenomena that matter, like shocks, sharp fronts, and fine-scale turbulence, are high-frequency. So a PINN representing the solution in space and time often just smooths those features out.

The third, and to me the most important, is that a PINN doesn't generalize. You train it for one initial condition, one set of parameters, one geometry. If you change any of those, you retrain from scratch. So you haven't really gained speed over a traditional numerical solver. In many cases you're slower and less accurate. For time-dependent problems, where you want to roll forward many scenarios, like weather forecasting or design exploration, that's a dealbreaker.

That's really what motivated our work on neural operators. Instead of learning a single solution function, you learn the solution operator, the map from input functions such as initial conditions, coefficients, or forcing to output functions. Because you work in function space, the model is resolution-invariant: you can train at one discretization and evaluate at another. And once it's trained, inference is extremely fast, which is how you get speedups of orders of magnitude, like what we've seen with FourCastNet for weather.

That doesn't mean physics constraints are useless. Physics-informed losses are valuable as an additional signal, for instance when you have limited data or want to fine-tune at higher resolution, as in physics-informed neural operators. You get the data-driven operator learning plus the PDE constraint, and the operator gives you a much better starting point, so the optimization doesn't get stuck the way a vanilla PINN does.

So my summary would be this. PINNs are a nice idea for inverse problems or for small, well-behaved systems. But for complex, time-dependent, multiscale physics, you need to learn at the level of operators and combine data with physics, not rely purely on the residual loss to do all the work.

r001.rationale: The response calls the optimization problem very ill-conditioned and says this difficulty worsens for time-dependent problems.

r002.rationale: It links turbulent flow with chaotic or multiscale systems and says trajectory errors propagate, but does not state that turbulent fluid dynamics become chaotic over sufficiently long time horizons.

r003.rationale: It says fine-scale turbulence is a physical phenomenon that matters and identifies turbulent flow as an example of chaotic or multiscale systems.

r004.rationale: The response describes the optimization as ill-conditioned and hard, but does not characterize solving a chaotic PDE from scratch across all times as unmanageable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the way I think about it is that physics-informed neural networks, PINNs, are really solving one instance at a time. You take a neural network, you parameterize the solution to the PDE, and you train it to satisfy the equation and the boundary conditions at a bunch of collocation points. That's elegant, but for time-dependent problems it runs into some fairly fundamental issues.

The first is that you're treating time as just another input coordinate. You're not propagating anything forward; you're trying to fit the entire spatiotemporal solution globally at once. That means the network has to simultaneously get the early dynamics right and the late dynamics right, and the late dynamics are only constrained through the PDE residual, not through any direct supervision. In practice, the optimization tends to find trivial or overly smooth solutions. For chaotic or multiscale systems, like turbulence or anything with sharp fronts, the error at early times compounds, and the loss landscape becomes very hard to navigate. You see spectral bias as well: these networks learn low frequencies first and struggle with the high-frequency content that time-dependent physics generates.

The second issue is the cost model. Every time you change the initial condition, the forcing, or a coefficient, you have to retrain from scratch. So you've essentially replaced a numerical solver with an optimization problem that's often slower and less reliable than the solver you started with. There's no amortization.

And the third thing is balancing the loss terms. You have an initial condition loss, boundary losses, and the residual loss, and their gradients live on very different scales. People have tried causal weighting, time marching, domain decomposition, and those help, but they're patches on top of a formulation that doesn't naturally respect causality.

That's really what motivated our work on neural operators. Instead of learning a single solution, you learn the map from input functions, like initial conditions, to output functions, so the model is learning the solution operator itself. Then time-dependent problems become autoregressive or directly learned in function space, you can be discretization-invariant, and you can still add physics losses, which is what we did in physics-informed neural operators. You get the generalization that PINNs lack, and you can be orders of magnitude faster than traditional solvers at inference time. I don't think PINNs are useless, they're great for inverse problems and data assimilation in a single setting, but for forecasting dynamics they're the wrong abstraction.

r001.rationale: The response describes PINN optimization as difficult for time-dependent problems, including a loss landscape that is “very hard to navigate.”

r002.rationale: It mentions chaotic systems and turbulence but does not state that turbulent fluid dynamics becomes chaotic over sufficiently long time horizons.

r003.rationale: It connects turbulence and chaotic or multiscale systems with sharp fronts and high-frequency content that PINNs struggle to learn, communicating the relevance of fine-scale effects.

r004.rationale: It says PINNs fit the full spatiotemporal solution globally, including chaotic or multiscale dynamics, and that the resulting loss landscape is very hard to navigate.

astra-6.text:
I think the key limitation is that putting the physics into the loss function doesn’t automatically make the optimization easy. In a physics-informed neural network, you typically represent the solution as a function of space and time, and penalize violations of the differential equation, the initial conditions, and the boundary conditions. Those objectives can compete during training.

For a time-dependent problem, causality matters: the state at a later time depends on getting the earlier evolution right. But if you optimize over the entire space-time domain at once, that causal structure isn’t necessarily reflected in the training procedure. You can have a small residual at the sampled points without accurately capturing the trajectory, especially over long time horizons or in systems where small errors grow rapidly.

That doesn’t mean physics-informed neural networks can’t work. Time windowing, causal training strategies, and better weighting of the loss terms can help. But we have to distinguish satisfying a sampled physics loss from obtaining a stable, accurate numerical solution.

There’s also an amortization question. With a conventional PINN, you often train again for a new initial condition or a new parameter setting. With neural operators, the goal is to learn the mapping across a family of problems, so that training can be reused. Physics constraints can be useful there too, but they don’t remove the need to assess stability and error over time.

r001.rationale: It says that putting physics in the loss does not automatically make optimization easy and that the objectives can compete during training.

r002.rationale: It mentions long horizons and systems where errors grow rapidly, but does not state that turbulent fluid dynamics becomes chaotic over time.

r003.rationale: It does not state that fine-scale effects matter in chaotic fluid dynamics.

r004.rationale: It describes optimizing over the full space-time domain as potentially missing causal structure, but does not characterize solving a chaotic PDE from scratch across all times as having an unmanageable optimization landscape.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key limitation is that putting the physics into the loss function doesn’t automatically make the problem easy to learn. In a typical physics-informed neural network, you represent the solution as a function of space and time, and penalize violations of the differential equation, the initial conditions, and the boundary conditions. But those different objectives can compete during optimization.

For time-dependent problems, causality matters. You need to get the earlier states right before you can accurately predict later states. A global space-time loss doesn’t necessarily respect that structure. You can have a small residual at sampled points and still have a poor trajectory, particularly over long time horizons or in systems where small errors grow rapidly.

There’s also a distinction between solving one instance and learning a family of problems. A conventional PINN often requires training again when you change the initial condition or a parameter. With neural operators, the goal is to learn the mapping from those inputs to the solution, so the training cost can be amortized across many instances. You can still incorporate physics into that training. But neither approach eliminates the need to check stability, accuracy, and generalization over time.
